phenotype: Two copies of the C282Y change
conclusion: You have two copies of the HFE change known as C282Y, one from each parent. The HFE gene helps control how much iron the body absorbs from food. C282Y is the name lab reports use for a change of one DNA letter in the HFE gene that stops the protein it makes from working properly. This is the pattern found in most people diagnosed with hereditary haemochromatosis, where the body slowly stores too much iron, and about 1 in 200 people of northern European ancestry have it. It is well established that by middle age most people with it have higher iron levels in the blood than people with two normal copies. Far fewer become ill: in a large study following people from middle age for about 12 years, about 28 in 100 men and 1 in 100 women with this result developed iron-related disease, which in that study counted raised liver enzymes (a blood sign that the liver is under strain) as well as liver damage or joint damage in the knuckles. Serious damage, such as scarring of the liver (cirrhosis), is much rarer: expert guidelines put it at about 4 in 100 people with this result, and between 5 and 6 in 100 men. Women are thought to be protected partly by monthly blood loss. Each of your brothers and sisters has about a 1 in 4 chance of having the same result. A blood test of iron levels (ferritin and transferrin saturation) shows whether iron is building up. If it is high, the usual treatment, regularly taking off some blood, is simple and prevents damage, and a doctor decides whether it is needed.

phenotype: One C282Y and one H63D change, on different copies
conclusion: You have one C282Y change and one H63D change in the HFE gene, one on each copy of the gene. The HFE gene helps control how much iron the body absorbs from food. You inherit one copy of the gene from each parent. C282Y and H63D are the names lab reports use for two changes of one DNA letter in this gene. One of your copies carries C282Y, which stops the protein the gene makes from working properly, and the other carries H63D, which changes the protein only slightly. Your iron levels are likely to run somewhat higher than those of people with two normal copies, but illness from iron is rare: in a large study following people from middle age for about 12 years, 1 of 82 men and none of 95 women with this combination developed iron-related disease. When people with it do build up too much iron, it is usually mild to moderate and usually comes with something else, such as heavy drinking or a fatty liver. About 2 in 100 people of northern European ancestry have this combination. A blood test of iron levels (ferritin and transferrin saturation) shows how your body is handling iron, and a doctor decides what, if anything, to do.

phenotype: C282Y and H63D on the same copy
conclusion: You carry the C282Y and H63D changes on the same copy of the HFE gene, and a normal version on the other copy. The HFE gene helps control how much iron the body absorbs from food. C282Y is the name lab reports use for a change of one DNA letter in the HFE gene that stops the protein it makes from working properly. H63D is the name lab reports use for a common one-letter change in the HFE gene whose effect on iron is small. This arrangement is very rare, because the two changes arose separately in human history and almost always sit on different copies of the gene. With one normal copy, this is expected to behave like carrying a single C282Y change, which does not raise the risk of hereditary haemochromatosis. The main way it matters is for children: a child who inherits this copy from you and a C282Y change from their other parent would have two C282Y changes, the pattern behind most hereditary haemochromatosis. This arrangement has not been studied directly, so the expectation rests on what is known about each change on its own.

phenotype: One copy of the C282Y change

Some carriers have slightly higher iron levels than people with two normal copies, but illness from iron overload is very rare and, when it happens, other genetic or lifestyle factors may be involved. The main way it matters is for children: a child who inherits your C282Y and another C282Y from their other parent would have two copies, the pattern behind most hereditary haemochromatosis.

phenotype: Two copies of the H63D change
conclusion: You have two copies of the HFE change known as H63D, one from each parent. The HFE gene helps control how much iron the body absorbs from food. phenotype: One copy of the H63D change
conclusion: You carry one copy of the HFE change known as H63D and one normal copy. The HFE gene helps control how much iron the body absorbs from food. conclusion: You have the C282Y change on both copies of the HFE gene, with an extra H63D change on one of them. The HFE gene helps control how much iron the body absorbs from food.
